questions.question: Filtration of waste products in humans happens in the kidneys. There is a large number of filtration units present inside the kidneys to help them in doing this job. These filtration units are called:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**nephrons**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Nephrons are the basic structural and functional units of the kidney.
 
• Each kidney contains around 1 to 1.5 million nephrons.
 
• Nephrons are responsible for the removal of waste products, excess substances, and toxins from the blood.
 
• They play a crucial role in the regulation of water, electrolytes, and maintaining the body's acid-base balance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Bowman's Capsule**

 
 
• The Bowman's capsule is a cup-like sac at the beginning of the nephron in the kidney.
 
• It encases the glomerulus and is involved in the first step of the filtration of blood to form urine.
 
• It captures the filtrate produced from the blood and passes it into the renal tubule.
 
 
 
• **Capillaries**
 
 
• Capillaries are the smallest blood vessels in the body.
 
• They facilitate the exchange of oxygen, carbon dioxide, nutrients, and waste products between blood and tissues.
 
• In the kidneys, capillaries are part of the glomerulus and play a critical role in the filtration process.
 
 
 
• **Alveoli**
 
 
• Alveoli are small air sacs in the lungs where gas exchange takes place.
 
• Oxygen from the inhaled air passes through the walls of the alveoli and into the blood in the capillaries, while carbon dioxide from the blood passes into the alveoli to be exhaled.
 
• They are crucial for efficient respiratory function but are not related to kidney function.

questions.question: Reflex arcs are formed in which part of the nervous system?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Spinal cord**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Reflex arcs are formed in the **spinal cord**, which is a part of the central nervous system.
 
• They are responsible for involuntary and nearly instantaneous movements in response to a stimulus.
 
• A reflex arc typically involves a sensory neuron, an interneuron, and a motor neuron, which facilitate the immediate reaction.
 
• The spinal cord acts as an intermediary, processing the reflex without involving the brain, thus saving time.
 
• Reflex actions help protect the body from harm, such as quickly withdrawing a hand from a hot surface.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Medulla**

 
 
• It is part of the brainstem that controls autonomic functions like breathing and heart rate.
 
• The medulla is not involved in the formation of reflex arcs but is critical for vital life functions.
 
 
 
• **Forebrain**
 
 
• This region includes structures such as the cerebrum and thalamus, involved in complex behaviors and cognitive functions.
 
• It does not play a direct role in reflex arcs.
 
 
 
• **Cerebellum**
 
 
• The cerebellum is responsible for coordinating voluntary movements and maintaining balance and posture.
 
• While important for motor control, it is not directly involved in reflex arcs.

questions.question: Which type of muscles do the uterus, iris of the eye, and bronchi contain?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Smooth muscles**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The uterus, iris of the eye, and bronchi contain **smooth muscles**.
 
• **Smooth muscles** are **involuntary, non-striated muscles** found in various internal organs.
 
• These muscles are responsible for various involuntary movements in the body such as the contraction of the uterus during childbirth, adjustment of the iris in response to light, and regulation of airflow in the bronchi.
 
• Unlike skeletal muscles, smooth muscles are not under conscious control and are regulated by the autonomic nervous system.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Striated muscles** include **skeletal muscles** that are under voluntary control and are characterized by their striped appearance.
 
• **Skeletal muscles** are attached to bones and help in body movements.
 
• **Cardiac muscles** are specialized **striated muscles found only in the heart**, responsible for pumping blood throughout the body.
 
• Smooth muscles are also found in the walls of blood vessels, digestive tract, and other hollow organs.

questions.question: Select the correct option related to the function regulated by ovaries.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Menstrual cycle**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The ovaries are responsible for producing hormones such as estrogen and progesterone, which are crucial for regulating the menstrual cycle.
 
• These hormones control the development and release of eggs (oocytes) from the ovaries during the menstrual cycle.
 
• The menstrual cycle is typically around 28 days long but can vary from person to person.
 
• The cycle consists of four main phases: menstruation, the follicular phase, ovulation, and the luteal phase.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Estrogen:** A hormone produced by the ovaries that plays a key role in the development of female secondary sexual characteristics and the regulation of the menstrual cycle.
 
• **Progesterone:** A hormone released by the corpus luteum in the ovary that prepares the endometrium for pregnancy if fertilization occurs.
 
• **Ovulation:** The process by which an ovary releases a mature egg into the fallopian tube, usually occurring around the midpoint of the menstrual cycle.
 
• **Menstruation:** The shedding of the uterine lining, resulting in bleeding, which marks the start of a new menstrual cycle.
 
• **Follicular Phase:** The phase of the menstrual cycle during which follicles in the ovary mature, ending with ovulation.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct related to male reproductive system?

options.text: Testes are located in the abdominal cavity.
Formation of sperm takes place in seminal vessel.
Sperm formation requires higher temperature than the normal body temperature.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Testes secrete testosterone hormone.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The testes are the primary male reproductive organs responsible for producing sperm and secreting the hormone testosterone.
 
• Testosterone is crucial for the development of male secondary sexual characteristics and the regulation of libido.
 
• The testes are located outside the abdominal cavity in the scrotum, which helps maintain a temperature slightly lower than the body temperature, essential for sperm production.
 
• Spermatogenesis, the process of sperm formation, occurs in the seminiferous tubules of the testes.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Seminal Vesicles:** These glands secrete a fluid that forms part of the semen and provides nutrients for the sperm.
 
• **Testosterone:** A steroid hormone produced by the Leydig cells in the testes, responsible for male sexual development and reproductive function.

questions.question: Other than the nervous system, which other system helps in control and coordination in our body?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Endocrine system**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The endocrine system consists of glands that secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream.
 
• These hormones regulate various bodily functions such as metabolism, growth, and mood.
 
• Major glands in the endocrine system include the pituitary, thyroid, adrenal, and pancreas.
 
• Hormones are chemical messengers that travel to target organs and tissues to exert their effects.
 
• The endocrine system works in conjunction with the nervous system to maintain homeostasis in the body.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Excretory system**

 
 
• Responsible for removing waste products from the body.
 
• Includes organs such as kidneys, ureters, bladder, and urethra.
 
 
 
• **Respiratory system**
 
 
• Responsible for the exchange of gases (oxygen and carbon dioxide) between the body and the environment.
 
• Includes organs such as the lungs, trachea, and bronchi.
 
 
 
• **Digestive system**
 
 
• Breaks down food into nutrients that the body can absorb and use for energy.
 
• Includes organs such as the stomach, intestines, liver, and pancreas.

questions.question: Which of the following hormones stimulates the development of ovarian follicles?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **FSH**

__Explanation:__

__
 
• Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) is a gonadotropin, a type of hormone that plays a crucial role in the reproductive processes of both males and females.
 
• In females, FSH is essential for the growth and maturation of ovarian follicles, which are the structures that contain the eggs.
 
• FSH is produced by the anterior pituitary gland and its release is regulated by the hypothalamus.
 
• FSH directly stimulates the development of ovarian follicles. It promotes the growth of the follicles in the ovary and the maturation of the oocytes (immature eggs) contained within them. This process is critical for ovulation and fertility.

**Other Options:**__

 
• **Estrogen:** Estrogen is produced by the growing follicles and helps regulate the menstrual cycle and prepare the uterine lining for pregnancy.
 
• **Progesterone:** Progesterone is primarily involved in preparing the uterine lining for implantation of a fertilized egg and maintaining early pregnancy.
 
• **LH (Luteinizing Hormone):** LH triggers ovulation, the release of a mature egg from the ovarian follicle. After ovulation, LH helps maintain the corpus luteum, which produces progesterone to support early pregnancy. However, LH does not stimulate the initial development of ovarian follicles.

questions.question: How many amino acids out of the 22 needed by the human body, are NOT produced in the human body?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**9**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Out of the 22 amino acids required for protein synthesis, **9 are considered essential amino acids** for humans because the body cannot synthesize them.
 
• These 9 essential amino acids must be obtained through the diet as they play a critical role in various physiological processes.
 
• The 9 essential amino acids are: **histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, and valine**.
 
• These amino acids are found abundantly in foods like **meat, fish, eggs, dairy products, soy, and quinoa**.
 
• The remaining 13 amino acids are classified as non-essential because the body can synthesize them from other compounds.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Amino Acids:**

 
 
• Amino acids are organic compounds that combine to form proteins, which are vital for the structure and function of cells.
 
• They consist of an amino group, a carboxyl group, and a side chain that varies between different amino acids.
 
 
 
• **Essential vs Non-Essential Amino Acids:**
 
 
• **Essential amino acids** cannot be synthesized by the body and must be obtained through diet.
 
• **Non-essential amino acids** can be produced by the body, even if they are not present in the diet.
 
 
 
• **Conditionally Essential Amino Acids:**
 
 
• Some amino acids, such as arginine, cysteine, and glutamine, are considered conditionally essential.
 
• Under certain conditions like illness or stress, the body may not produce enough of these amino acids, making dietary intake necessary.
 
 
 
• **Protein Sources:**
 
 
• Animal-based foods (e.g., meat, fish, eggs, and dairy) are considered complete proteins as they provide all 9 essential amino acids.
 
• Plant-based foods (e.g., beans, lentils, and nuts) can be combined to form complete protein profiles.
 
 
 
• **Role of Amino Acids:**
 
 
• Amino acids are critical for processes like enzyme production, tissue repair, and nutrient absorption.
 
• They also play roles in hormone synthesis, immune function, and energy production.

questions.question: Which of the following receptors help in the detection of taste?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gustatory receptors**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Gustatory receptors are specialized sensory receptors responsible for detecting taste.
 
• These receptors are located on the taste buds found on the tongue, soft palate, and epiglottis.
 
• Taste buds contain gustatory cells that respond to different taste stimuli such as sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami.
 
• When gustatory cells are stimulated by tastants, they send signals to the brain via the gustatory pathway to interpret different tastes.
 
• The detection and differentiation of tastes play a crucial role in dietary choices, nutrition, and overall health.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Olfactory receptors**

 
 
• These receptors are responsible for the detection of smell.
 
• Located in the olfactory epithelium within the nasal cavity, they respond to odor molecules.
 
 
 
• **Photoreceptors**
 
 
• These are specialized cells in the retina that respond to light.
 
• Photoreceptors include rods and cones, which are essential for vision.
 
 
 
• **Phonoreceptors**
 
 
• These receptors are involved in detecting sound.
 
• They are primarily found in the cochlea of the inner ear and are crucial for hearing.

questions.question: Which part of brain is responsible for respiration?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Medulla oblongata**

**__Concept:__**

__
 
• The brain can be divided into three parts the forebrain, the midbrain, and the hindbrain.
 
• The brain sends and receives chemical and electrical signals throughout the body.
 
• It controls the voluntary movements, and balance of the body, (functioning of vital involuntary organs lungs, heart, and kidneys).
 
• The forebrain consists of the cerebrum, thalamus, and hypothalamus.
 
• The hindbrain comprises the pons, cerebellum, and medulla.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/8b9b3ceb4ec2845223ade9281a6837d6e3bcc038d4a7206f9ad2c6fbd095607a.png] 

**Explanation:**__

 
• **Medulla oblongata:** The medulla oblongata is the lower part of the brainstem.

 
 
• It plays a crucial role in regulating vital functions such as heart rate, blood pressure, and respiration.
 
• The medulla contains centres which control respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretions.
 
• The medulla oblongata contains the respiratory centers (the dorsal respiratory group and the ventral respiratory group) that control the rate and depth of breathing by sending signals to the respiratory muscles.
 
 
 
• **Pons:** The pons is located above the medulla oblongata and also plays a role in respiration.
 
 
• It contains the pneumotaxic center and the apneustic center, which help regulate the rhythm of breathing.
 
• However, it is not the primary center for controlling respiration, making it an incorrect answer compared to the medulla oblongata.
 
 
 
• **Cerebrum:** The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain and is responsible for higher brain functions such as thought, memory, and voluntary muscle movements.
 
• **Gyri:** Gyri are the ridges or folds on the surface of the cerebral cortex.
 
 
• They increase the surface area of the brain and are involved in various functions depending on their location.
 
• Gyri are not directly involved in the control of respiration, making this an incorrect answer.

questions.question: What is the medical term for high blood pressure?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Hypertension**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Hypertension** is the medical term for high blood pressure.
 
• It is a condition where the **force of the blood against the artery walls is too high**.
 
• Hypertension is often referred to as a **silent killer** because it may not show any symptoms for years.
 
• It can lead to serious health complications like **heart disease, stroke, and kidney failure**.
 
• Common causes include **genetic factors, poor diet, lack of physical activity, and stress**.
 
• Management includes **lifestyle changes** such as a balanced diet, regular exercise, and medications as prescribed by healthcare providers.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Hypotension**__

 __
 
• **Hypotension** is the medical term for low blood pressure.
 
• It can cause symptoms like **dizziness, fainting, and fatigue**.
 
• Severe hypotension can be life-threatening, leading to shock.
 
 
 
• **Hyperglycemia**__
 __
 
• **Hyperglycemia** is the medical term for high blood sugar levels.
 
• It is commonly associated with **diabetes**.
 
• Symptoms include **increased thirst, frequent urination, and fatigue**.
 
 
 
• **Hypoglycemia**__
 
 
• **Hypoglycemia** refers to low blood sugar levels.
 
• It can cause symptoms such as **shakiness, sweating, confusion, and irritability**.
 
• If untreated, it can lead to **seizures, unconsciousness, or even death**.

questions.question: Which of the following transports food, carbon dioxide and nitrogenous wastes in a dissolved form?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Plasma**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Plasma** is the liquid component of blood that transports nutrients, hormones, and proteins to the parts of the body that need it.
 
• It makes up about **55% of the body's total blood volume**.
 
• Plasma carries carbon dioxide, which is a waste product of cellular metabolism, from tissues to the lungs for exhalation.
 
• It also transports nitrogenous wastes to the kidneys for excretion.
 
• Plasma helps maintain blood pressure and regulates body temperature.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Blood Composition**

 
 
• Blood consists of cells suspended in plasma: red blood cells (RBCs), white blood cells (WBCs), and platelets.
 
• RBCs are responsible for oxygen transport, WBCs are involved in immune response, and platelets play a key role in blood clotting.
 
 
 
• **Functions of Plasma**
 
 
• Plasma serves as a medium for transporting nutrients, waste products, and other substances throughout the body.
 
• It contains clotting factors that help prevent excessive bleeding during injury.
 
• Plasma proteins, like albumin, help maintain osmotic balance and transport hormones, vitamins, and drugs.
 
 
 
• **Carbon Dioxide Transport**
 
 
• Carbon dioxide is primarily transported in the blood in the form of bicarbonate ions (HCO3-).
 
• A smaller amount is dissolved directly in plasma, and some bind to hemoglobin in red blood cells.
 
 
 
• **Nitrogenous Wastes**
 
 
• Nitrogenous wastes like urea and creatinine are byproducts of protein metabolism.
 
• These wastes are carried by plasma to the kidneys, where they are filtered out and excreted in urine.

questions.question: Which of the following is the correct order of movement of food in the digestive tract?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mouth - Oesophagus - Stomach**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **Mouth (Oral Cavity):**
 
• The digestive process initiates in the mouth, serving as the entry point for food.
 
• Mechanical digestion occurs through mastication (chewing), breaking down food into smaller particles, increasing surface area.
 
• Salivary glands, located in the mouth, secrete saliva, which contains enzymes like salivary amylase.
 
• Salivary amylase begins the chemical digestion of carbohydrates, specifically starch, into simpler sugars.
 
• The tongue manipulates food, forming a bolus, a rounded mass of chewed food.
 
• The tongue also plays a role in taste perception, detecting flavors through taste buds.
 
• The process of swallowing begins when the bolus is pushed towards the pharynx.
 
• The mouth prepares the food for further digestion by adding moisture and enzymes.
 
• The teeth are essential for the mechanical breakdown of food.
 
• The oral cavity is lined with mucous membrane, which helps lubricate food.
 
• **Oesophagus (Esophagus):**
 
• The oesophagus is a muscular tube approximately 25 centimeters long in adults.
 
• It connects the pharynx to the stomach, acting as a conduit for food passage.
 
• Peristalsis, a series of rhythmic muscle contractions, propels the bolus downward.
 
• These wave-like muscle movements ensure unidirectional movement of food towards the stomach.
 
• The lower esophageal sphincter, a muscular ring at the junction of the oesophagus and stomach, prevents the backflow of stomach acid.
 
• The oesophagus is lined with a mucous membrane that aids in the smooth passage of food.
 
• The walls of the oesophagus contain both circular and longitudinal muscle layers.
 
• The movement of the bolus is largely involuntary.
 
• The oesophagus passes through the diaphragm.
 
• The oesophagus is essential for transporting the bolus from the oral cavity to the stomach.
 
• **Stomach:**
 
• The stomach is a muscular, J-shaped organ that acts as a temporary storage and digestion site.
 
• It secretes gastric juices, including hydrochloric acid (HCl), pepsinogen, and mucus.
 
• HCl creates an acidic environment (pH 1.5-3.5), which activates pepsinogen to pepsin.
 
• Pepsin, a protease enzyme, breaks down proteins into smaller peptides.
 
• The stomach's muscular walls churn and mix the food with gastric juices, forming chyme.
 
• Mucus protects the stomach lining from the corrosive effects of HCl.
 
• The stomach's capacity is approximately 1 liter, allowing for the storage of ingested food.
 
• The stomach also absorbs some substances, such as water, alcohol, and certain medications.
 
• The stomach has folds called rugae, which allow it to expand.
 
• The stomach has three muscle layers: longitudinal, circular, and oblique.

questions.question: Excessive production of which of the following hormones in the body causes the Cushing's syndrome, leading to weight gain and thinning of the skin?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Cortisol**__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Cushing's syndrome i**s caused by an excess of the hormone cortisol.
 
• Cortisol **is a glucocorticoid hormone produced by the adrenal glands.**
 
• Cushing's syndrome** is a hormonal disorder that occurs when the body produces too much cortisol over a long period of time. **
 
• **Cortisol is sometimes called the "stress hormone" because it helps the body respond to stress**. 
 
• Symptoms include weight gain, thinning skin, and a round, red face. 
 
• Cushing's syndrome can be serious if left untreated. ​

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Melatonin **

 
 
• **​**Melatonin, **an indoleamine, is a natural compound produced by various organisms,** including bacteria and eukaryotes.
 
• Its** discovery in 1958 by Aaron B. Lerner** and colleagues stemmed from the isolation of a substance from the pineal gland of cows that could induce skin lightening in common frogs
 
 
 
• **Vasopressin**
 
 
• **​**A **hormone that helps blood vessels constrict and helps the kidneys control **the amount of water and salt in the body.
 
• This helps **control blood pressure and the amount of urine that is made. **
 
• **Vasopressin is made by a part of the brain called the hypothalamus **and is secreted into the blood by the pituitary gland.
 
 
 
• Erythropoietin 
 
 
• **Erythropoietin **(EPO) is a hormone that helps the body maintain a healthy red blood cell count. It's produced in the kidneys and released into the bloodstream when oxygen levels are low. 
 
 

9f:T

questions.question: When the level of growth hormone is low, which releases growth hormone releasing factor and stimulates the pituitary gland to release growth hormone?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Hypothalamus**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Hypothalamus**
 
• The hypothalamus is a region in the brain that plays a crucial role in regulating hormone release.
 
• When growth hormone levels are low, the hypothalamus releases **growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH)**.
 
• GHRH then stimulates the **pituitary gland** to secrete **growth hormone (GH)**.
 
• This process is part of the feedback mechanism that maintains hormonal balance in the body.
 
• The hypothalamus also releases **somatostatin**, which inhibits GH release when levels are sufficient.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Thyroid Gland:**
 
• The thyroid gland produces hormones like **thyroxine (T4)** and **triiodothyronine (T3)**, which regulate metabolism.
 
• It does not directly influence the release of growth hormone or growth hormone-releasing factor.
 
• The thyroid gland is regulated by the **thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)** from the pituitary gland.
 
• Dysfunction in the thyroid gland can affect growth indirectly by altering metabolic rates.
 
• However, it is not involved in the direct release of growth hormone-releasing factor.
 
• **Adrenal Gland:**
 
• The adrenal glands produce hormones like **cortisol**, **adrenaline**, and **aldosterone**.
 
• These hormones are involved in stress response, blood pressure regulation, and electrolyte balance.
 
• The adrenal glands do not produce or regulate growth hormone-releasing factor.
 
• They are regulated by the **adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)** from the pituitary gland.
 
• While cortisol can influence growth indirectly, it is not part of the growth hormone release mechanism.
 
• **Pancreas:**
 
• The pancreas is primarily responsible for producing **insulin** and **glucagon**, which regulate blood sugar levels.
 
• It does not play a role in the release of growth hormone or growth hormone-releasing factor.
 
• The pancreas is part of the endocrine and digestive systems but is not involved in the hypothalamic-pituitary axis.
 
• Insulin-like growth factors (IGFs) are influenced by growth hormone but are not produced by the pancreas.
 
• The pancreas has no direct connection to the regulation of growth hormone release

questions.question: The lactic acid that gets accumulated in the muscle cells during rigorous exercise causing muscle cramps is produced from
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Pyruvate**

__Explanation:__

__
 
• During intense physical activity, such as rigorous exercise, the oxygen supply to muscle cells may not be sufficient to meet the energy demands of the body.
 
• This leads to anaerobic respiration in muscle cells, where glucose is partially broken down to generate energy in the form of ATP.
 
• In the absence of sufficient oxygen, pyruvate (a product of glycolysis) is converted into lactic acid by the enzyme lactate dehydrogenase.
 
• The accumulation of lactic acid in muscle cells is responsible for muscle cramps and fatigue during prolonged or intense exercise.

Pyruvate is a key intermediate in cellular respiration.

 
• In the presence of oxygen (aerobic conditions), pyruvate enters the mitochondria and is converted into acetyl-CoA for the citric acid cycle.
 
• However, under anaerobic conditions, pyruvate is converted into lactic acid in muscle cells to regenerate NAD⁺, which is essential for glycolysis to continue and produce ATP. This process is called **lactic acid fermentation.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/53ab19d383740216219a4c1847307c262f1ec29cbead09c95669dc8efca7d212.png] 

**Other Options:**__

 
• **ATP:** ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the energy currency of the cell. It is produced during glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation. ATP is not directly converted into lactic acid; rather, its production is facilitated by glycolysis, where pyruvate is formed as an intermediate.
 
• **Ethanol:** Ethanol is a byproduct of fermentation in certain microorganisms, such as yeast. It is not produced in human muscle cells. Humans undergo lactic acid fermentation, not alcoholic fermentation, under anaerobic conditions.
 
• **Glucose:** Glucose is the primary source of energy in cellular respiration. It undergoes glycolysis to produce pyruvate, which can subsequently be converted into lactic acid under anaerobic conditions.

questions.question: Harmful metabolic wastes from our body are removed by the biological process called:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**excretion**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Excretion** is the biological process by which harmful metabolic wastes are removed from the body.
 
• This process is vital for maintaining homeostasis and preventing damage to the body from the accumulation of toxic substances.
 
• In humans, the major excretory organs include the kidneys, liver, lungs, and skin.
 
• The kidneys filter blood to produce urine, which carries waste products out of the body.
 
• The liver processes toxins and waste products, converting them into less harmful substances that can be excreted.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Defecation**

 
 
• This is the process of eliminating solid waste (feces) from the digestive tract through the anus.
 
• It is different from excretion, as it involves the removal of undigested food and other non-metabolic waste.
 
 
 
• **Secretion**
 
 
• This involves the production and release of substances such as enzymes, hormones, and mucus by glands and cells.
 
• Secretion plays a role in various bodily functions but is not primarily involved in waste removal.
 
 
 
• **Transportation**
 
 
• This refers to the movement of substances such as nutrients, gases, and wastes within the body.
 
• While essential for overall bodily function, transportation is not a process that directly removes metabolic waste.
